_help: Per commodity, an indicator->1-5 map (5 = bullish). A bare number or {"score": n, "note": "why"} for auditability. Unset = held at neutral and excluded from the average, exactly like fundamentals_manual. Refreshed by the fx-strength-desk-daily task, step 2c.

Real yield direction.note: Headwind intensified: the 10-year jumped a fifth straight session to 5.01% on 15 Sep (briefly 5.04%), its first touch of 5% since July 2007, as markets lock in an ~88-92% probability of a 25bp hike at today's (16 Sep) FOMC. That is a materially bigger drag than the ~4.85% level scored a week ago.

US dollar direction.note: DXY firmed to 99.57 on 15 Sep, its highest since 3 Sep, tracking the yield spike into the FOMC. A firmer headwind than the high-98s scored a week ago, though the hike itself is now largely priced so the reaction into tomorrow's statement is the swing risk.

Central-bank & ETF demand.note: Both legs now pulling the same way. WGC data: global gold ETFs added US$18bn in August (second-largest monthly inflow on record) and Q3 is the strongest quarter on record - the Western-outflow risk flagged on 6 Sep has clearly reversed, inflows are running hard through the hawkish-Fed repricing. Central banks still accumulating above official net-purchase reports; 2026 sell-side targets ($4,900-6,000 year-end) rest on continued official buying. Not a 5 only because gold is at record highs and chasing here carries drawdown risk.

Safe-haven bid.note: Bid is losing the tug-of-war with rates: gold slipped to a six-week low near $4,263 on 15 Sep (-1.2% on the day) even with Strait of Hormuz tensions still unresolved - the 5% 10-year and firmer dollar are now outweighing the haven bid rather than being offset by it, a reversal from the 10 Sep read.

Real yield direction.note: Same intensified headwind as gold - 10-year hit 5.01% on 15 Sep, first time since July 2007, with an ~88-92% priced hike at today's FOMC. Silver is more leveraged to the move than gold.

US dollar direction.note: DXY at 99.57 (15 Sep), highest since 3 Sep, firming into the FOMC alongside the yield spike. Firmer headwind than a week ago.

Industrial demand.note: Structural pull still firm: Silver Institute-based 2026 estimates put industrial demand on track to exceed 720 Moz (a record), with solar PV alone near 175-185 Moz (up from ~50 Moz in 2015) and electronics/EV around 300-310 Moz - against roughly flat ~830 Moz/yr mine supply, extending a structural deficit into its sixth year. But broader 2026 global growth is still soft (IEA's Sept OMR has 2026 oil demand down 2.5 mb/d, a bigger contraction than last month), which caps the cyclical industrial pull even as the structural story stays strong. Net mildly positive, unchanged.

Gold-silver ratio.note: Ratio ~65 (XAU ~4470 / XAG ~68.4), compressed further from ~67.5 a week ago and well below the long-run ~80 average - silver has already closed most of the gap to gold and is no longer cheap on this measure. Neutral for further silver outperformance.

OPEC+ supply policy.note: Still the 6 Sep decision - the seven core OPEC+ members PAUSED output increases, holding October quotas at the September level (31.01 Mb/d) after four straight monthly hikes, wanting to set 2027 baselines first while Hormuz disruption limits the group's ability to move price anyway. No new OPEC+ meeting since (next is 4 Oct), so the supportive 'no more barrels coming' read is unchanged and reconfirmed, not stale.

Inventory trend.note: API reported a small crude draw (~-0.3 Mb) for the week ending 4 Sep; the EIA weekly report was pushed to 12:00/14:00 ET on 10 Sep by the 7 Sep federal closure. The mid-August build had already fully reversed and EIA's STEO expects stocks near/below the 5-year low through year-end on strong exports and low imports. August PPI energy +4.2% underlines the tight physical picture. Slightly tight.

Demand outlook.note: Refreshed to the September IEA Oil Market Report (out this week): 2026 demand now forecast down 2.5 mb/d - about 940 kb/d worse than last month's read - though the pace of decline is easing quarter to quarter (5.3 mb/d in Q2 to an expected 2 mb/d in Q4). Weaker than the prior ~-80 kb/d estimate, so demand is a bigger drag than previously scored. Current price strength (North Sea Dated spiked to $113.48/bbl on 9 Sep) is supply/risk-premium and inventory-draw driven (observed stocks down 507 mb since February), not demand - keep this leg separate from the inventory/geopolitical legs which are correctly capturing that strength.

Geopolitical risk premium.note: Still elevated with a fresh escalation: Saudi Arabia shut a major East-West pipeline, on top of the ongoing US-Iran Strait of Hormuz tensions (no ceasefire, shipping attacks, proposed transit-toll regime). WTI has jumped roughly 15% this month toward $99-100. Holding at 4.5 - already near the top of the range.
